listenings.text: Hi Tiago, it's Denise from purchasing. I'll be quick. We need the bracket two millimetres thinner on the next order. Same length, same holes, just thinner. I know we approved the current spec back in May, so yes, this is a change, and yes, it is short notice. Can you tell me by Thursday if that works? If it doesn't work, tell me what does, because I do need something different from what we have now. Call me, please. Don't send an email, I will not read it today.

post_skill.title: What do you think?
items: Denise says what she wants, but not why. Is that normal where you work?
She asks for a call, not an email. Why would she do that?
If you call her back, what is the first thing you say?
Suppose you simply do what she asked. What could go wrong?
Who in your company would say yes to this before checking anything?

language.label: Target language — the questions that open a request

Can I ask what's driving this?

Would it help if...?

language.title: Six of them do six different jobs. Match each line to its job.
words: "Before I confirm, can I check one thing?"
"Do you mean lighter, or physically smaller?"
"Would it help if we shipped fewer per box?"
defs: turns a vague request into a choice between two things
tests another way without promising it
asks for the reason behind the request
closes with a date instead of a promise
says the requirement back in your own words

language.text: Notice what is missing from the whole bank: "No problem, I can do that." Every line here asks, checks, offers or commits to a date. Agreeing before you understand feels like good service, and it is the most expensive mistake in this job.

pre_comm.title: Reveal answer key
list: Can I ask what's driving this? It would help me find the best way.
Do you mean lighter, or physically smaller?
So what you need is a lighter box, not a thinner part.
Before I confirm, can I check one thing with the factory?
Would it help if we shipped fewer pieces per box?
pre_comm.note: Accept justified variations. After each one, say it out loud: which sounds more natural in your voice?

items: The setup
Your teacher is Denise, from the customer's purchasing team. She left you the voicemail you heard, and you are calling her back. She wants the bracket two millimetres thinner.
Information gap

Denise answers ONLY as Denise, and only what you ask. She will not volunteer the reason behind the request. Your job is to find it by talking to her — not by guessing, and not by explaining the factory to her.
Your goal

Leave the call knowing (1) what problem she is really solving, (2) what would count as a solution for her, and (3) what you committed to, and by when. Do not offer anything before you know the first two.

task1.label: Useful language
items: Can I ask what's driving this?
What happens if we don't?
Just to be clear...
Do you mean lighter, or physically smaller?
So what you need is...
Would it help if...?
That one I'd have to check with the factory.
I'll confirm by Thursday.
Leave it with me.
Case 1 — "Send it faster"
A customer asks you to ship on Tuesday instead of Friday. The truck is already booked for Friday and moving it costs about nine hundred dollars.
Case 2 — "We want a second supplier"
Your main customer says they are looking for a second supplier for your part. They ask you for the full spec so they can share it.
Case 3 — "Just make a few extra"
The customer asks for twenty extra pieces, free, "for testing". It is the third time this year.

task2.title: For each case, out loud
items: Which question would you ask FIRST, and why that one?
What would you NOT say, even if you are thinking it?
What is the smallest thing you could offer that still solves their problem?
Say the whole first sentence of your answer, in one breath.

task2.text: Your teacher will disagree with one of your three answers and push back. Hold your position in English — or change it, and say why you changed it.

feedback.title: Focus on accuracy
items: At what moment in the call did you know what Denise actually needed?
Which question got you there — and which one wasted time?
Say one sentence you got stuck on. Say it again now, slowly, the way you wanted it.
Where in your week could you use "Can I ask what's driving this?" — and what would probably come out?
